sections.h2: How should a Texas seller read the city and county guides?
sections.html:
Read the county guide for the place your house sits in first, because the appraisal district, tax office and clerk that touch your sale are all organized by county. Then use the city page for neighborhood facts, local permits and market context.

Texas covers 261,267.85 square miles of land, according to Census QuickFacts, and has 254 counties. Harris County has over 4 million residents and Loving County just over 100, so staffing, office hours and wait times differ a great deal even though the statutes are identical.

sections.h2: Who sets and collects property tax in Texas?
sections.html:
No state body taxes real estate here. Counties, cities, school districts and special districts each set a rate, and two separate offices handle the money side.

  • The appraisal district, run by a chief appraiser under a board, assigns value and handles exemptions.
  • An appraisal review board listens to owners who dispute a value.
  • The county tax assessor-collector commonly bills and collects for several units at once.

In counties with 75,000 or more people the assessor-collector holds a seat on the district board as an ex officio member. A seller often needs both offices: one for exemption status, the other for a payoff figure.

sections.h2: Which property tax dates matter most to a seller?
sections.html:
Five recurring dates shape most closings, as the Comptroller's deadline calendar prints them.

Five dates a Texas seller can circle
WhenEvent
January 1Appraisal day, when value, exemption status and the year's lien are fixed
April 1 or soon afterValue notices reach single-family homesteads
May 15Protest cutoff for most owners (a later 30-day window applies if the notice came late)
October 1Bills go in the mail
February 1Anything still unpaid is delinquent

Owners may also split a bill, paying half by November 30 and the rest by June 30 of the following year.

sections.h2: What does a late Texas tax bill cost?
sections.html:
Delinquency brings a six percent penalty plus one percent interest right away. Penalty then grows a point monthly to a 12 percent level in July, while interest keeps climbing with no cap.

Collection attorneys hired by a unit may add up to 20 percent. A payment plan is available to homestead owners, and some collectors run it for 36 months. Title companies want a written payoff, so request one from the tax office.

sections.h2: Where does the county clerk fit into a sale?
sections.html:
Think of the clerk as the county's keeper of title records: deeds, deeds of trust, releases, liens, foreclosure notices, plus probate filings and small estate affidavits. Filing happens in the land's county, whatever your home address.

A deed needs a signature and an acknowledgment before it can be filed, and the clerk publishes the fee schedule. Call ahead of closing.

sections.h2: How does Texas foreclosure shape a quick sale?
sections.html:
Typical Texas deeds of trust let the lender sell without a lawsuit. The borrower has 20 days from the default notice to reinstate; the lender then posts notice at least 21 days before an auction on a first Tuesday.

Selling before the auction lets you pay the lender out of the price. A deficiency suit after the auction must start within two years. The State Law Library foreclosure guide walks through each stage, and a housing counselor can help before a date is set.

sections.h2: What do eviction and squatter rules mean for owners?
sections.html:
Landlords bring eviction suits in justice court after a written notice, normally three days. Trial comes soon: service at least four days ahead, a hearing within 10 to 21 days of filing, and a five-day window to appeal.

Property Code Chapter 24B gives owners a faster option against some squatters, a request to the sheriff or constable with no court case. It excludes family members and current or former tenants, and requires that the property was closed to the public when entered.

sections.h2: How do probate and inheritance affect a Texas house?
sections.html:
Wills go to probate within four years of a death, usually where the person lived. Simple estates have lighter options, namely muniment of title, small estate affidavit and affidavit of heirship.

With the inheritance tax gone since 2015, heirs mostly face property tax and recording steps. Only very large estates meet the federal return threshold, listed by the IRS at $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths.

sections.h2: How do Texas counties differ from one another for sellers?
sections.html:
Size is the biggest difference. A county with millions of residents runs large offices with online search, while a county of a few hundred people may keep records in a single courthouse room.

Expect variation in the following areas, and ask each office directly.

  • Whether a local option homestead exemption has been adopted by the county, city or school district.
  • How the tax office takes payments and issues written payoffs.
  • Which days a clerk accepts documents for recording and what it charges.
  • Where foreclosure and tax sale notices are posted and sales held.

The state statutes set the floor, and local decisions add to it.

sections.h2: What paperwork should a Texas seller gather first?
sections.html:
A missing page can delay a closing, so collect these before listing.

  • The latest notice of appraised value from the appraisal district.
  • This year's tax statement with a written payoff.
  • The recorded deed showing how you took title.
  • Evidence of each exemption now on the property.
  • Any lien release, court order or affidavit that a past estate or loan left behind.

If a document is missing, the county clerk can usually supply copies of anything recorded, and the appraisal district can confirm exemptions on file.

sections.h2: Which Texas guides fit which situation?
sections.html:
Match the guide to the problem you are solving, and expect to read more than one.

  • Behind on taxes or facing a bill you think is wrong: the property tax and protest material, plus your county page.
  • Inherited a house: probate, heirship and homestead pages, plus the county clerk guide.
  • Behind on a mortgage: the foreclosure material and the sale-before-auction option.
  • Landlord with a difficult occupant: the eviction and squatter pages.
  • Curious about value: the housing market page with FHFA and Census data.

Each guide names the official page it draws on, so you can check a rule or date at the source before you act on it.

sections.h2: Why does Texas exempt so many homeowners from part of the tax?
sections.html:
Homesteads get a mandatory $140,000 school exemption, older or disabled owners get $60,000 on top, and appraised value on a homestead may grow 10 percent yearly at most. Disabled veterans get exemptions tied to a VA rating, up to a full exemption at 100 percent.

Those rules shape what a buyer inherits when a house changes hands. Exemptions attach to the person who applied. A buyer files a new application, generally before May 1; the seller's status does not carry over.

sections.h2: What happens if a Texas property goes to a tax sale?
sections.html:
A yearly lien lets a court order a delinquent property sold, even after it changes hands. A constable or the unit's agent runs the auction; ask the county for notices.

Buy-back rights run two years for homestead, farm and mineral property, at a 25 percent premium in the first year and 50 percent in the second. Other land gets roughly 180 days. Money left after the sale is open to the former owner for two years.

faqs.q: How many counties does Texas have?
faqs.a: 254, from Harris County with over 4 million residents down to Loving County with just over 100, according to the Comptroller's county page.

faqs.q: Is there a state-level property tax in Texas?
faqs.a: None. Rates come from local units, and the appraisal district fixes values on January 1.

faqs.q: Who gives me a tax payoff figure?
faqs.a: The county tax assessor-collector, or the collector your taxing unit hires. The appraisal district handles value and exemptions, not payment.

faqs.q: Where is a deed recorded after a sale?
faqs.a: At the clerk in the land's county, after the deed is signed and acknowledged. Ask that office for current fees.
No, it ended September 1, 2015. The federal return threshold for 2026 deaths is $15,000,000.
